items.stem: When a class implements an interface, how many of the interface's members must it provide?

options.text: Only the properties, not the methods
None — the interface provides default bodies for everything

items.explanation: An interface is a contract; the implementing class must supply every member (the compiler enforces it).

misconceptions.a: Picking a subset would break the contract and fail to compile.

items.stem: What is the role of `ISink<T>` in Synnduit?

options.text: A concrete class that writes to the destination
A contract that your destination connector class must fulfill

items.explanation: ISink<T> is an interface (a contract); your sink class implements it, supplying all its members.

misconceptions.a: ISink<T> is the contract; the concrete class (e.g. StaffSink) is what implements it.

items.stem: Why can the Synnduit engine call any connector you write without knowing your concrete class?

options.text: It reads your source code at runtime
It talks to your class through the interface (IFeed<T> / ISink<T>) it implements
All connectors must be named the same
It copies your class into the engine

items.explanation: Because your class fulfills the interface contract, the engine can call it polymorphically through that interface — that's the value of programming to an interface.

items.stem: A teammate writes `class StaffSink : ISink<Staff>` but only implements Create and Update. What will happen and why?
rubric: Because ISink<Staff> is a contract requiring all its members (New/Create/Get/Update/Delete) to be implemented
items.sampleAnswer: It won't compile — implementing ISink<Staff> obligates the class to provide every member of the interface, not just Create and Update. The missing members are a compile error.
